definition: fair to everyone; not favoring one side over another

hero.text: When Bolt and Pixel argued over whose plan to use, Juniper stayed impartial and judged both plans by the same rules.

everyday: A good referee stays impartial, even when her cousin is playing on one of the teams.

contrast.nonExample: The judge of the art contest gave first prize to her best friend's painting without looking closely at the others.
contrast.explanation: An impartial judge treats every side the same way. Favoring a friend is the opposite of impartial.

items.prompt: Which person is being impartial?

options.text: A debate judge who cheers whenever her own school's team speaks.
A teacher who grades every essay with the same rubric, without looking at names.
A coach who lets his son start every game.
A reporter who interviews only people who agree with her.

items.hint: Look for the person who treats every side the same way.
items.explanation: Impartial means not favoring anyone. Grading with the same rubric and hiding names keeps the teacher from playing favorites.

wrong.a: Cheering for her own school shows she favors one side.
wrong.c: Always starting his son is favoritism.
wrong.d: Hearing only one side is one-sided, not impartial.

items.prompt: The prefix im- means "not." Partial can mean "favoring one side." So impartial most likely means…
items.hint: Put "not" in front of "favoring one side."
items.explanation: Im- (not) + partial (favoring one side) = not favoring any side. "Partly finished" uses a different meaning of partial that doesn't fit here.

wrong.a: That is another meaning of partial (incomplete), but impartial is about fairness.
wrong.b: That is what partial means, without the "not."
wrong.d: An impartial person can decide; they just decide fairly.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The two towns had argued about the river for years. To settle it, they hired a mediator from far away, someone with no land, friends, or family in either town. They wanted someone truly ___.
items.clue: no land, friends, or family in either town
items.hint: Why would it matter that the person had no ties to either town?
items.explanation: Having no land, friends, or family in either town means the mediator has no reason to favor one side. That is impartial. Experienced might be nice, but the clue is about having no connections.

wrong.c: The passage stresses having no ties, not having skill.
wrong.d: The mediator came from far away, the opposite of local.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what impartial means.

chunks.text: scored the projects without seeing students' names.
gave extra points to their own students.

items.hint: Which ending keeps the judges from favoring anyone?
items.explanation: Hiding names stops judges from favoring students they know, which keeps them impartial. Giving extra points to their own students is bias.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "impartial" in this sentence?
items.passage: Historians try to write impartial accounts, describing what each side in a war believed instead of choosing heroes and villains.
items.hint: What do you call an account that picks a side?
items.explanation: Biased means leaning toward one side, the opposite of impartial. Neutral is a synonym, not an opposite. An account can be detailed or accurate and still be biased.

wrong.c: Neutral means nearly the same as impartial.

definition: doubting that something is true until you see good evidence

hero.text: Rex was skeptical when a stranger claimed his gadget could make anyone fly, so he asked to see it tested first.

everyday: Mara was skeptical of the ad promising that the cream would cure acne overnight.

contrast.nonExample: Theo believed the online rumor right away and shared it with everyone he knew.
contrast.explanation: A skeptical person questions a claim and wants proof. Believing something instantly is the opposite.

items.prompt: Is Dev being skeptical?
items.passage: A website said a new drink makes people grow two inches taller. Dev said, "I'd want to see a real study before I believe that."
items.hint: Does Dev believe the claim right away, or does he want evidence?
items.explanation: Yes. Dev doubts the claim and asks for evidence first. Being skeptical means not believing until there is good proof.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the scientists' reaction?
items.passage: When a lab announced it had built a machine that runs forever without fuel, most scientists did not call the claim impossible right away. They simply asked to see the data and wanted other labs to repeat the test.
items.clue: asked to see the data; wanted other labs to repeat the test
items.hint: They didn't reject it outright, and they didn't believe it either.
items.explanation: The scientists doubted the claim but stayed open, asking for data. That is skeptical. Dismissive would mean rejecting it without checking, which the passage says they did not do.

wrong.d: Dismissive means waving something away; these scientists wanted to check.
wrong.c: Amazed people would believe it; these wanted proof.
wrong.a: Nothing shows anger.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The candidate promised to lower taxes and build three new schools at the same time. Voters who remembered last year's broken promises were ___, wondering where the money would come from.
items.clue: remembered last year's broken promises; wondering where the money would come from
items.hint: How would you feel about a promise if the last ones were broken?
items.explanation: Remembering broken promises and wondering about the money shows the voters doubted the claim. That is skeptical.

wrong.b: Confident voters would believe the promise.
wrong.a: Grateful means thankful; they haven't received anything.

items.prompt: Which line uses "skeptical" correctly?

options.text: "I'm skeptical that this old map is real. The paper looks brand new."
"I'm skeptical about the trip, so I packed my bag a week early!"
"She was so skeptical that she believed every word he said."
"The skeptical puppy wagged its tail at everyone."

items.hint: Look for someone who doubts something and gives a reason.
items.explanation: The speaker doubts the map and points to evidence (new-looking paper). That is skeptical. Believing every word is the opposite.

wrong.b: Packing early shows excitement, not doubt.
wrong.c: Believing every word is trusting, not skeptical.
wrong.d: Wagging at everyone shows friendliness, not doubt.

items.prompt: What does "skeptical" mean in this passage?
items.passage: In 1912, Alfred Wegener argued that the continents had once been joined. Many geologists were skeptical; they asked what force could possibly move entire continents. Only decades later did new evidence change their minds.
items.clue: asked what force could possibly move entire continents; new evidence change their minds
items.hint: What finally changed the geologists' minds?
items.explanation: The geologists questioned the idea and changed their minds only when new evidence arrived. Skeptical means doubtful until shown proof.

wrong.a: They asked questions; nothing shows insults.
wrong.d: They did not agree at first.

definition: to say or show the opposite of something, so that both cannot be true

hero.text: Kai said the lab was empty all night, but the security video contradicted him: it showed someone sneaking in at midnight.

everyday: The new fossil evidence contradicted the old idea that the dinosaur had no feathers.

contrast.nonExample: Lin said it rained on Tuesday, and the weather report also showed rain on Tuesday.
contrast.explanation: To contradict, two statements must disagree. When the report matches what Lin said, it supports her instead.

items.prompt: Contra- means "against" and dict means "say." What does contradict most likely mean?

options.text: to say the opposite of something

items.hint: Combine "against" with "say."
items.explanation: Contra (against) + dict (say) = to say against, or say the opposite. You see dict in dictionary and predict too.

wrong.a: Saying again would be repeating, not going against.
wrong.c: That is closer to dictate.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In his report, Omar wrote that the Titanic sank in 1915. His own source, a museum website, ___ him: it clearly listed the date as 1912.
items.clue: clearly listed the date as 1912
items.hint: Do the two dates match or disagree?
items.explanation: Omar wrote 1915, but the source said 1912. The source says the opposite of what he wrote, so it contradicted him. Confirmed would mean it agreed.

wrong.c: Confirmed means agreed with; the dates don't match.
wrong.b: The source did not repeat his date.

items.prompt: Does the second statement contradict the first?
items.passage: First: "Our school has the most students in the district." Second: "Our school has more students than any other school in the district."
items.hint: Do the two sentences disagree, or say the same thing in different words?
items.explanation: No. Both statements mean the same thing, so they agree. To contradict, the statements must be opposite so that both cannot be true.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what contradict means.

chunks.text: The witness said the car was red,
by showing the same red car.

items.hint: To contradict, the photo has to show something different.
items.explanation: A blue car is the opposite of what the witness said, so the photo contradicts her. Showing the same red car would support her.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "contradicts" in this sentence?
items.passage: The mayor says the park is safe at night, but the police report contradicts her claim.
items.hint: What would the report do if it agreed with the mayor?
items.explanation: Supports means backs up a claim, the opposite of contradicts. Questions is weaker than contradicts but goes in the same direction.

wrong.c: Questioning a claim leans toward contradicting it, not the opposite.
wrong.a: Ignoring the claim is neither agreeing nor disagreeing.

definition: seeming reasonable and likely to be true

hero.text: Pixel's guess that the power outage came from the storm was plausible, since lightning had struck near the station.

everyday: "The bus was late" is a plausible excuse on a snowy morning.

contrast.nonExample: Jake told his teacher a dragon flew off with his homework.
contrast.explanation: A plausible explanation could reasonably be true. A dragon story is not believable at all.

items.prompt: Which explanation is the most plausible?
items.passage: The cookies on the counter are gone, and there are crumbs leading to the dog's bed.

options.text: Aliens beamed the cookies into space.
The cookies melted into the counter.
A tiny wizard turned them invisible.

items.hint: Which explanation could reasonably be true, given the crumbs?
items.explanation: Plausible means reasonable and likely. The crumbs lead to the dog's bed, so "the dog ate them" makes sense. The others are not believable.

wrong.a: That is not believable.
wrong.d: Wizards are not a reasonable explanation.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the detective's view of the story?
items.passage: The suspect said he was at the library all afternoon. The detective thought this could be true, since the man had a library card and a stack of books, but she still planned to check the sign-in sheet.
items.clue: could be true; still planned to check
items.hint: The story seems reasonable, but she hasn't confirmed it yet.
items.explanation: The detective thinks the story is reasonable but not yet confirmed. Plausible means likely or believable. Proven and certain are too strong, since she still wants to check.

wrong.a: Proven goes too far; she still needs to check.
wrong.d: Certain is too strong for something she plans to double-check.
wrong.b: Ridiculous means not believable at all, but she thinks it could be true.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Early astronomers noticed that ships seemed to sink below the horizon hull-first. The idea of a round Earth seemed ___, because a curved surface would hide the bottom of a ship before the top.
items.clue: because a curved surface would hide the bottom of a ship before the top
items.hint: The sentence gives a reason the explanation makes sense.
items.explanation: The "because" clause explains why a round Earth makes sense of what sailors saw. A reasonable, believable explanation is plausible.

wrong.c: The explanation clears up the mystery rather than adding one.
wrong.d: The explanation helps, so it isn't useless.

items.prompt: Is this a plausible excuse?
items.passage: Asked why he missed soccer practice, Ian said, "I was building a rocket to visit Mars with my little sister."
items.hint: Could this reasonably be true?
items.explanation: No. A kid building a rocket to Mars is not believable. A plausible excuse is one that could reasonably be true, like a dentist appointment.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "plausible" in this sentence?
items.passage: The author makes the time-travel plot feel plausible by explaining the science step by step.
items.hint: Why would explaining the science step by step matter to readers?
items.explanation: Explaining the science makes readers think the plot could happen. Believable matches plausible. Scientific describes the method, not the effect on readers.

wrong.d: The science is how the author does it; plausible describes the result: it seems believable.
wrong.a: A plot can be exciting without being believable.

definition: an opponent or enemy; someone you compete or struggle against

hero.text: In the academy chess final, Nova faced her toughest adversary: Bolt, who had never lost a match.

everyday: The two senators were adversaries in the election but shook hands after the results came in.

contrast.nonExample: Rosa and her lab partner worked together to finish the experiment.
contrast.explanation: An adversary is on the opposite side. A lab partner is working with you, so she is an ally, not an adversary.

items.prompt: In which sentence is one person acting as an adversary?

options.text: Ella's coach helped her practice her serve.
In the debate, Mason argued against Priya's side.
Leo's teammate passed him the ball.

items.hint: An adversary is on the other side.
items.explanation: Mason argues against Priya, so he is her opponent, her adversary. A coach, teammate, and grandmother are all on Ella's or Leo's side.

wrong.a: A coach helps you, not opposes you.
wrong.c: A teammate is an ally.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: During the American Revolution, Britain and France had been enemies for decades. That long history helps explain why France chose to help the colonists against its old ___.
items.clue: enemies for decades; against
items.hint: What do you call a country you've been enemies with for a long time?
items.explanation: "Enemies for decades" tells you Britain was France's long-time opponent, its adversary. Neighbor is true on a map, but it misses the clue about being enemies.

wrong.d: The clue is about being enemies, not location.
wrong.a: Partners work together; these countries were enemies.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "adversary" in this sentence?
items.passage: In the courtroom, the two lawyers were adversaries, but outside they were old friends.
items.hint: What do you call someone who is on your side?
items.explanation: An ally is on your side, the opposite of an adversary. Rival is a synonym. A judge is neutral, not an ally.

wrong.b: A rival is nearly the same as an adversary.
wrong.c: A judge stays neutral; that isn't the opposite of opponent.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what adversary means.
items.hint: Whom would a player study before a match?
items.explanation: A player studies her opponent's serve to prepare, so "adversary" fits. A cheering teammate is on her side, not an adversary.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the snake in this passage?
items.passage: For the young mongoose, the cobra was a dangerous foe. The two circled each other, each waiting for the other to make the first mistake.
items.clue: dangerous foe; circled each other
items.hint: "Foe" is a clue. What are the two animals doing?
items.explanation: "Dangerous foe" and circling each other show the cobra is the mongoose's opponent, its adversary. Victim suggests the cobra is helpless, but it is dangerous.

wrong.c: A dangerous foe is not helpless.
wrong.a: A companion keeps you company; these animals are fighting.

definition: to make a problem, pain, or worry less severe

hero.text: Juniper planted trees along the hot street to alleviate the summer heat for the people who lived there.

everyday: An ice pack can alleviate the swelling from a sprained ankle.

contrast.nonExample: Wearing shoes that were too tight made Ari's blisters worse.
contrast.explanation: To alleviate is to make something less bad. Making blisters worse is the opposite.

items.prompt: Does this action alleviate the problem?
items.passage: The cafeteria line was so long that students had only five minutes to eat. The principal opened a second serving line, and the wait was cut in half.
items.hint: Did the problem get less severe?
items.explanation: Yes. Opening a second line made the long wait less severe. To alleviate means to ease or lessen a problem, even if it isn't completely gone.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: After the drought destroyed local crops, volunteers trucked in rice and clean water. The supplies did not end the crisis, but they helped ___ the families' hunger for several weeks.
items.clue: did not end the crisis, but they helped
items.hint: The supplies helped, but they didn't end the problem.
items.explanation: "Did not end the crisis, but they helped" shows the hunger became less severe but did not disappear. Alleviate means to lessen. Eliminate would mean ending it completely, which the passage rules out.

wrong.d: Eliminate means to remove entirely, but the passage says the crisis did not end.
wrong.a: Rice and water would not make hunger worse.

items.prompt: Which word fits best?
items.passage: The new bike lanes will not solve the city's traffic problems, but planners hope they will ___ some of the rush-hour crowding.
items.clue: will not solve; some of
items.hint: The lanes won't fix everything. Which word means to make it partly better?
items.explanation: "Will not solve" and "some of" tell you the lanes should make crowding less bad, not end it. Alleviate fits. Cure is too strong, since it means fixing completely.

wrong.a: Cure means to fix completely; the passage says the lanes won't solve it.
wrong.b: Planners don't want to create crowding.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what alleviate means.

chunks.text: Hana drank three cups of coffee.

items.hint: Which action would make nervousness less severe?
items.explanation: Deep breathing calms nerves, so it alleviates them. Lots of coffee would likely make her jitterier, the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "alleviate" in this sentence?
items.passage: The town built a second bridge to alleviate the pressure on the old one, which was starting to crack.
items.hint: What would a second bridge do to the load on the first?
items.explanation: A second bridge takes some traffic away, easing the pressure on the old one. Ease matches alleviate. Repair would mean fixing the cracks, which a new bridge doesn't do.

wrong.d: The new bridge reduces the load; it doesn't fix the cracks.

definition: chosen or decided without a good reason or fair rule, as if at random

hero.text: The villain's rules were arbitrary: one day hats were banned, the next day shoes, and nobody knew why.

everyday: Students complained that the new seating chart felt arbitrary, since the teacher gave no reason for it.

contrast.nonExample: The coach picked the starting team based on who scored best in practice drills.
contrast.explanation: An arbitrary choice has no clear reason. Choosing by practice scores follows a clear, fair rule.

items.prompt: Which decision is arbitrary?

options.text: The library closes at 6 because that is when the last bus leaves.
A class picks a field-trip site by voting.
The manager fires a worker just because he dislikes her shirt color.
The pool closes during lightning for safety.

items.hint: Which decision has no good reason behind it?
items.explanation: Firing someone over a shirt color has no good reason, so it is arbitrary. The other decisions are based on buses, a vote, or safety.

wrong.a: The bus schedule is a real reason.
wrong.d: Safety is a good reason.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In some ancient kingdoms, a ruler could jail anyone for any reason, or for no reason at all. Documents like the Magna Carta tried to protect people from this kind of ___ punishment.
items.clue: for any reason, or for no reason at all
items.hint: What do you call punishment given for no reason?
items.explanation: "For no reason at all" is the defining clue. Punishment without a fair reason or rule is arbitrary. Lawful would mean following rules, the opposite.

wrong.d: Lawful punishment follows rules; this had none.
wrong.c: Whether it was public isn't the point of the clue.

items.prompt: Is the teacher's choice arbitrary?
items.passage: Ms. Kato sets the essay length at 500 words because that's how long the state test essay will be.
items.hint: Does she have a reason?
items.explanation: No. Ms. Kato has a clear reason: matching the state test. An arbitrary choice has no real reason behind it.

items.prompt: Which line uses "arbitrary" correctly?

options.text: "The rule is arbitrary because the safety experts tested it for years."
"My arbitrary dog always comes when I call."
"He was so arbitrary that he finished his homework early."
"Why must the line form on the left? That seems totally arbitrary."

items.hint: Which speaker is pointing out a rule with no clear reason?
items.explanation: The speaker can't see any reason for the line rule, so calling it arbitrary fits. A rule tested for years has a strong reason, so it isn't arbitrary.

wrong.a: Years of testing give the rule a reason, so it is not arbitrary.
wrong.b: Arbitrary describes choices or rules, not reliable pets.
wrong.c: Finishing early is about effort, not random choices.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "arbitrary" in this sentence?
items.passage: In the math problem, you may pick an arbitrary number for x; the pattern works no matter which one you choose.
items.clue: no matter which one you choose
items.hint: If any number works, how do you choose it?
items.explanation: In math, arbitrary means any choice at all, picked at random. Unfair doesn't fit here, since nobody is being treated badly by choosing a number.

wrong.c: Arbitrary can suggest unfairness in rules, but in this math sentence it just means any number at all.
wrong.d: Any number works, so there isn't one correct number.

definition: to express an idea or feeling clearly in words

hero.text: After the rescue, Kai struggled to articulate how scared he had been, but finally he found the right words.

everyday: In her essay, Zoe articulated three clear reasons the school should start later.

contrast.nonExample: Asked why he liked the book, Max just shrugged and said, "I dunno, it was good."
contrast.explanation: To articulate an idea is to put it into clear words. A shrug and "I dunno" do not express a reason clearly.

items.prompt: What does "articulate" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Before the debate, Nadia practiced articulating her main argument in just two sentences.
items.hint: Why would she practice saying it in just two sentences?
items.explanation: Nadia is practicing putting her argument into clear, short words. That is what articulate means.

wrong.a: Memorizing is different from expressing an idea clearly.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Jonah knew the painting made him feel something, but he couldn't ___ what. After staring at it for ten minutes, he finally wrote, "It feels lonely, like the last day of summer."
items.clue: finally wrote, "It feels lonely…"
items.hint: He had the feeling already. What was hard was putting it into…
items.explanation: Jonah had the feeling but struggled to put it into words, then finally wrote it down. Articulate means to express clearly in words. Imagine doesn't fit, because the feeling was already there.

wrong.b: He already felt it; the struggle was finding words.
wrong.d: He was staring for ten minutes, so he wasn't ignoring it.

items.prompt: Did Carmen articulate her concern?
items.passage: At the town meeting, Carmen stood up and said, "The crosswalk near the school has no light, and two kids were almost hit last month. We need a signal there."
items.hint: Did she say clearly what the problem was and what she wanted?
items.explanation: Yes. Carmen named the problem, gave evidence, and said what she wanted, all in clear words. That is articulating a concern.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what articulate means.

chunks.text: In his speech, the class president
so clearly that everyone understood them.
so quietly that no one could follow.

items.hint: Articulating means expressing clearly. Which ending matches?
items.explanation: Expressing goals so clearly that everyone understood shows articulating. If no one could follow, the goals weren't expressed clearly.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "articulated" in this sentence?
items.passage: The Declaration of Independence articulated ideas about rights that many colonists already believed but had never seen written so plainly.
items.clue: already believed but had never seen written so plainly
items.hint: The colonists already believed the ideas. What did the document do with them?
items.explanation: The ideas already existed; the Declaration expressed them clearly in writing. Invented is wrong because the passage says colonists already believed them.

wrong.a: The colonists already believed the ideas, so the document didn't invent them.
wrong.d: The document stated the ideas; it didn't question them.

definition: kind and wanting to help or do good for others

hero.text: The benevolent old inventor gave Pixel her best tools for free, saying only, "Use them to help people."

everyday: A benevolent neighbor shoveled the walks of every older person on the block after the blizzard.

contrast.nonExample: The landlord raised the rent on his poorest tenants just because he knew they couldn't move.
contrast.explanation: A benevolent person wants good things for others. Taking advantage of people is the opposite.

items.prompt: Bene- means "good" and vol means "wish." A benevolent person most likely…
items.hint: Put "good" and "wish" together.
items.explanation: Bene (good) + vol (wish) = wishing good. A benevolent person wishes good things for others. You see bene in benefit, too.

wrong.c: Getting wishes is luck, not kindness.
wrong.d: Bene means good in the sense of doing good, not skill.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the queen?
items.passage: The young queen lowered taxes during the famine, opened the royal storehouses to hungry families, and built free hospitals. Even her critics admitted she seemed to truly care for her people.
items.clue: opened the royal storehouses; built free hospitals; truly care for her people
items.hint: Polite describes manners. What describes actions that do real good?
items.explanation: Feeding the hungry and building free hospitals show she wanted to do good for others, so benevolent fits. Polite is only about good manners, which is much weaker.

wrong.d: Polite is about manners; her actions go much further than that.
wrong.a: She may be wealthy, but the clues describe her kindness.

items.prompt: Is this an example of a benevolent act?
items.passage: A company donated money to a children's hospital, but only so it could put its logo on the building and sell more products.
items.hint: Look at why the company gave the money.
items.explanation: No. The company's main goal was selling more, not helping others. Benevolent describes a real wish to do good, not giving for advertising.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In the novel, everyone fears the old hermit on the hill. At the end, readers learn he has secretly been leaving food on the doorsteps of poor families for years. He was ___ all along.
items.clue: secretly been leaving food on the doorsteps of poor families
items.hint: What does leaving food for poor families show about him?
items.explanation: Secretly feeding poor families shows a kind wish to help, so he was benevolent. He might be lonely or mysterious, but the clue is about his kindness.

wrong.c: He seemed mysterious, but the ending reveals kindness.
wrong.a: The ending shows the fear was wrong.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "benevolent" in this sentence?
items.passage: The fairy tale's benevolent godmother helps the girl escape, while her stepmother plots against her.
items.hint: Think of the stepmother, who plots against the girl.
items.explanation: Malicious means wanting to cause harm, the opposite of benevolent, which means wanting to do good. Magical and elderly describe the godmother but are not opposites.

wrong.b: Magical isn't about kindness at all.
wrong.d: Shy is about confidence, not kindness.

definition: honest and direct, even when the truth is uncomfortable

hero.text: Rex was candid with the team: "My plan failed, and it was my fault."

everyday: Lucia asked for a candid opinion of her poem, so her friend told her the ending felt rushed.

contrast.nonExample: When asked if he'd broken the vase, Owen changed the subject and talked about the weather.
contrast.explanation: A candid person speaks openly and honestly. Dodging the question is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which response is the most candid?
items.passage: A friend asks, "Did you like my band's concert?" You thought the songs were great but the sound was too loud.

options.text: "The songs were great, but honestly, the sound was way too loud."

items.hint: Which answer is honest and direct about both the good and the bad?
items.explanation: Candid means honest and direct. This answer shares the real opinion, including the uncomfortable part about the sound.

wrong.a: "Perfect" isn't honest, since you thought the sound was too loud.
wrong.b: Changing the subject avoids the question.
wrong.d: Refusing to answer is guarded, not candid.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the coach's feedback?
items.passage: "You have real talent," the coach told Asha, "but you skip drills, and right now that's why you're on the bench." It stung, but Asha appreciated that he didn't sugarcoat it.
items.clue: didn't sugarcoat it; appreciated
items.hint: The feedback was honest and direct, but was it meant to hurt?
items.explanation: The coach was honest and direct without trying to be mean, and Asha appreciated it. That is candid. Rude would mean disrespectful, but he also praised her talent.

wrong.a: Rude suggests disrespect, but the coach was fair and Asha appreciated it.
wrong.c: His feedback was specific, not vague.
wrong.d: Flattering would hide the hard truth.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In her memoir, the scientist is surprisingly ___ about her failures. She describes experiments that went wrong, grants she was denied, and a mistake that cost her lab a year of work.
items.clue: describes experiments that went wrong, grants she was denied, and a mistake
items.hint: She openly describes her failures. What word fits that kind of honesty?
items.explanation: She openly shares her failures instead of hiding them, so she is candid. Secretive is the opposite, and boastful would mean bragging about successes.

wrong.a: She shares her failures openly, the opposite of secretive.
wrong.b: Boastful people brag; she admits mistakes.

items.prompt: Which line uses "candid" correctly?

options.text: "Let me be candid: I don't think we can finish the project by Friday."
"He was so candid that he lied about his grades."
"She stayed candid by hiding her real feelings."

items.hint: Look for a speaker about to share an honest, maybe unwelcome, truth.
items.explanation: "Let me be candid" introduces an honest, direct statement that may be unwelcome. Lying or hiding feelings is the opposite of candid.

wrong.b: Lying is the opposite of candid.
wrong.c: Candid describes people or statements, not taste (candied, with an e, means coated in sugar).
wrong.d: Hiding feelings is guarded, not candid.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "candid" in this sentence?
items.passage: In a candid interview, the retired player admitted that he had often been jealous of his teammates.
items.clue: admitted that he had often been jealous
items.hint: He admitted something embarrassing. What kind of interview is that?
items.explanation: Frank means openly honest, like candid. Admitting jealousy is an honest, uncomfortable truth. Private describes who hears it, not how honest it is.

wrong.c: Private is about audience, not honesty.
wrong.a: Length has nothing to do with honesty.
